newsitem.title: UK: BOE STG PROJECTION SEEN AS ATTEMPT TO TALK IT DOWN.
newsitem.headline: BOE STG PROJECTION SEEN AS ATTEMPT TO TALK IT DOWN.

text.p: The Bank of England's projection of a decline in sterling's trade weighted index over the next two years highlights efforts by the central bank to talk down the currency, analysts say.

On its own, analysts said on Wednesday such an assumption was unsurprising but it was noteworthy the Bank of England Deputy Governor Mervyn King drew attention to it at a presentation of the bank's August inflation report.

Joe Prendergast, currency strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London, said the Bank was hardly likely to project a stronger pound. " But it is interesting that he mentioned it, which has made it more important."
King said the central bank was assuming a good part of sterling strength would unwind over the next two years with the trade weighted index falling back to 90. It currently trades around 101.

This assumption fits with growing market expectations of higher rates in Europe, particularly in Germany, and a flattening rate outlook for Britain, which is seen taking away some of the yield attraction of investing in sterling.
"They're really talking about cyclical interest rate factors for sterling," said James McKay, international economist at PaineWebber in London.

Sterling's trade weighted index, which has a base year of 1990, was last around 90 in October last year when sterling/mark stood around 2.47 marks and sterling/dollar was around $1.63. Sterling currently stands at 2.9005 marks and $1.5810.
"The Bank is trying to talk sterling down. Economists and traders had been continually rolling over their expectations for UK rate hikes and the bank is trying to quash that," McKay said

And analysts said this assumption of a sterling fall can be seen as another dose of verbal intervention which started last week following comments by the Bank of England as it raised official rates to 7.0 percent from 6.75 percent.
At the time, the Bank said, "Upward pressure on the exchange rate should be reduced by the perception that interest rates have reached a level consistent with the inflation target."
Sterling fell sharply across the board last week after the bank's comments, easing some of the concerns corporate Britain was expressing about the effect the pound was having on exports.
Sterling, prior to its recent setback, had set an eight-year high of 3.0878 marks in July. This followed about a year of steady appreciation in the sterling/mark rate.

"Today's comments could be seen as another indication that sterling did get to overvalued levels and it's not really news that officials in the UK think sterling is too strong," said Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago in London.
